answer.sourceLine: Iacocca wrote it, and it is not buried anywhere: it is the fourth sentence of his 2007 book Where Have All the Leaders Gone?, written with Catherine Whitney. We read it in context in the publisher-permitted reproduction of chapter one ↗, which carries the line “Source: Where Have All the Leaders Gone? Chapter 1: Had Enough? ©2007 by Lee Iacocca. All Rights Reserved. Used by permission.” Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ cites the same book (Scribner, 2007).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Where Have All the Leaders Gone?
Chapter 1, “Had Enough?” — the fourth sentence of the book

source.excerpt: Am I the only guy in this country who's fed up with what's happening? Where the hell is our outrage? We've got a gang of clueless bozos steering our ship of state right over a cliff, we've got corporate gangsters stealing us blind, and we can't even clean up after a hurricane much less build a hybrid car. But instead of getting mad, everyone sits around and nods their heads when the politicians say, “Stay the course.”
trail: We read the sentence in its own paragraph in a reproduction of the book’s first chapter ↗ that states its provenance explicitly: “Source: Where Have All the Leaders Gone? Chapter 1: Had Enough? ©2007 by Lee Iacocca. All Rights Reserved. Used by permission.” The wording matches the popular version word for word.

Wikiquote’s Lee Iacocca page ↗ lists the fuller passage — through “This is America, not the damned Titanic” — and sources it to Where Have All the Leaders Gone? (2007), Scribner, ISBN 1416532471. Two independent routes, one book.
Wikipedia’s article on the book ↗ confirms the 2007 publication and the co-author credit to Catherine Whitney, and summarises the leadership framework the rest of the book hangs on.
The internal evidence fits. The chapter has Iacocca writing “Lee, you’re eighty-two years old” in his friends’ mouths; he was born on 15 October 1924 ↗, which makes him 82 through most of 2007.
source.excerptNote: The book’s opening paragraph, as reproduced by permission ↗. One sentence has been elided for length — “We should be screaming bloody murder” sits between the second and third sentences above. What follows the paragraph is the line the book was sold on: “Stay the course? You’ve got to be kidding. This is America, not the damned Titanic. I’ll give you a sound bite: Throw the bums out!”
source.rightsNote: Firmly in copyright. The book was first published in 2007 and the chapter excerpt we verified against carries the notice “©2007 by Lee Iacocca. All Rights Reserved.” Quoted here for identification and comment; quotle.info makes no public-domain claim.

author.name: Lee Iacocca
author.heading: About Lee Iacocca
author.metaLine: 1924–2019 · American automobile executive — Ford Mustang, Ford Pinto, and the Chrysler rescue
author.bio: Lido Anthony “Lee” Iacocca was the most famous car executive of his generation: the man behind the Ford Mustang, the driving force behind the Ford Pinto, president of Ford from December 1970 until Henry Ford II fired him in July 1978, and then for fourteen years the chairman who pulled Chrysler back from collapse. He was also a bestseller twice over. Iacocca: An Autobiography made him a household name in 1984; this book, at 82, was the angry one.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the sound of an eighty-two-year-old industrialist deciding he has nothing left to lose. The sentence arrives fourth, before any argument has been made — the chapter ↗ opens “Am I the only guy in this country who’s fed up with what’s happening? Where the hell is our outrage?” and then swings. Iacocca had spent a long career being quoted as the voice of American business. He used the last of that credit on a tirade.

The targets are all 2007, and he names them in the same chapter: a president he accuses of ignoring the Constitution and leading the country to war “on a pack of lies,” tax cuts for the wealthy (“thanks, but I don’t need it”), business leaders famous for being “the guys in handcuffs,” a press “waving pom-poms instead of asking hard questions,” and the failure to clean up after Hurricane Katrina.
detailsBody: The line most people remember from the passage is the one right after it: “This is America, not the damned Titanic. I’ll give you a sound bite: Throw the bums out!” Iacocca knew exactly what he was doing — he says so, in the chapter, in those words: I’ll give you a sound bite.

He was making the same argument about his own industry that spring. In a Morning Edition interview on 26 April 2007 ↗ he told Steve Inskeep that Detroit had been slow to notice the market had moved, and called for “something like the Manhattan Project” to get America off fossil fuels. The book’s complaint about not being able to “build a hybrid car” is the same thought, in his angrier register.
context.pull: You can’t call yourself a patriot if you’re not outraged.

sourcesVerified.claim: A reproduction of chapter 1 of Where Have All the Leaders Gone?, headed "Had Enough? BY LEE IACOCCA", contains verbatim: "We've got a gang of clueless bozos steering our ship of state right over a cliff, we've got corporate gangsters stealing us blind, and we can't even clean up after a hurricane much less build a hybrid car." It is the fourth sentence of the book.

The same page carries the provenance line "Source: Where Have All the Leaders Gone? Chapter 1: Had Enough? (c)2007 by Lee Iacocca. All Rights Reserved. Used by permission." — establishing both the work and its copyright status.

The same chapter contains "Stay the course? You've got to be kidding. This is America, not the damned Titanic. I'll give you a sound bite: Throw the bums out!", the passage about the President being "given a free pass to ignore the Constitution", "the guys in handcuffs", the press "waving pom-poms", "You can't call yourself a patriot if you're not outraged", and the friends' line "Lee, you're eighty-two years old."
Wikiquote's Lee Iacocca page lists the fuller passage (through "This is America, not the damned Titanic.") and sources it to Where Have All the Leaders Gone? (2007), Scribner, ISBN 1416532471.
Wikipedia states the book was published in 2007 and credits it to "Lee Iacocca & Catherine Whitney".
Wikipedia gives Iacocca's birth date as October 15, 1924 and death as July 2, 2019, president of Ford December 10, 1970 - July 13, 1978, and at Chrysler November 2, 1978 - December 31, 1992.

NPR's Morning Edition of April 26, 2007, "Iacocca Says Detroit Is Living in the Past", has Iacocca telling Steve Inskeep that Detroit has been slow to realize the market has changed; Wikiquote quotes him there calling for "something like the Manhattan Project" to "get off fossil fuels".
